Mehmet Oz, MD 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
 
Re: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage 
Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Childrenâ€™s Health 
Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified 
Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges (CMS-0062-P) 
 
Dear Dr. Oz: 
 
On behalf of the American Urological Society (AUA), thank you for the opportunity to submit 
comments on the Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed rule. 
 
The AUA is a globally engaged organization with more than 22,000 members practicing in 
more than 100 countries. Our members represent the worldâ€™s largest collection of expertise 
and insight into the treatment of urologic disease. Of the total AUA membership, more than 
18,000 are based in the United States, therefore we are actively engaged in commenting on 
the regulatory proposals of the Department of Human and Health Services and its agencies 
that affect our members and their patients. Our members provide invaluable support to the 
urologic community by fostering the highest standards of urologic care through education, 
research, and formulation of health policy 
 
We are grateful that we can participate in the rule making process, and we recognize the 
Medicare & Medicaid Servicesâ€™ (CMS) and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health 
Information Technologyâ€™s efforts to reduce administrative burden on providers. The AUA 
appreciates the opportunity to comment on CMSâ€™s proposed policies to advance 
interoperability and improve prior authorization processes. AUA members and other medical 
providers continue to report that prior authorization requirements impose significant 
administrative burdens on physicians and their staff, while also delaying patientsâ€™ timely 
access to medically necessary treatments, procedures, and medications. 
 
The AUA believes that use of prior authorization in any form will continue to place undue 
burden on providers while disrupting and interfering with the shared decision-making 
process between providers and their patients. We believe that shared decision making is 
fundamental to the provider and patient relationship and is vital to improved health 
outcomes. If CMS is going to proceed with the policies promulgated in this rule, the following 
comments outline our concerns. 
 
Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Following extensive stakeholder feedback on the 2024 Interoperability and Prior 
Authorization rule, CMS proposed in this rule to expand interoperability and electronic prior 
authorization requirements to include prescription drugs, addressing a key recommendation 
from commenters. As one of the stakeholders who made that request, we appreciate the 
agency's efforts to modernize electronic prior authorization (ePA) processes and support 
policy that reduces the administrative burden associated with current manual workflows. We 
 
believe that adopting  standardized ePA processes and improving interoperability has the 
potential to make the prior authorization system more efficient for patients and providers, 
ultimately supporting more timely access to the drugs and therapies that patients with 
urologic conditions and diseases need. 
 
This proposed expansion of ePA represents an important and necessary advancement in 
reducing barriers to care. Recent AUA membership survey data found that 93 percent of 
respondents indicated that medications they prescribe require prior authorization. Many of 
these medications are critical to the treatment and management of overactive bladder, erectile 
dysfunction, low testosterone, cancer, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. Delays in access to 
these therapies can negatively affect patient outcomes, quality of life, and continuity of care. 
The AUA strongly supports the inclusion of physician-administered drugs within the scope of 
these policies, including drugs furnished in physician offices such as chemotherapy and other 
infused or injected therapies. Delays in authorization for cancer treatments and other time-
sensitive therapies can have serious clinical consequences for patients. We also recommend 
the clinical indications for time-sensitive therapies and rapid prior authorization decisions be 
standardized across plans. Applying standardized ePA requirements and timelines to 
physician-administered drugs will help ensure that patients receive medically necessary 
treatment without avoidable delays. 
 
Understanding that the agency wanted the plans to retain flexibility and autonomy by NOT 
developing an exhaustive list of drugs that require prior authorization, the AUA would like to 
recommend that, at a minimum, the agency consider standardizing drug classes that require 
prior authorization. A standardized list may decrease administrative burden since providers 
will then be able to streamline their workflows as they will have upfront information 
regarding the drugs they are prescribing. This knowledge will allow the provider to 
proactively be informed when making prescribing decisions for their patients. 
 
Reporting Metrics and Decision Timeframes 
We support CMSâ€™s proposed timelines for prior authorization decisions requiring decisions 
for standard requests be available in 72 hours and expedited requests in 24 hours. However, 
certain clinical situations may require even faster decisions. Many urologists seek prior 
authorizations for CT or MRI scans for patients prior to a diagnosis. For example, a patient 
with an acute stone that is obstructing a kidney carries a significant morbidity in up to 60%.1 
This condition can cause significant pain, infectious complications, and renal insufficiency in 
the affected patient. If a provider is unable to get approval for these services in time, lifesaving 
treatments and surgeries are further delayed and can detrimentally impact the patient and 
their quality of life. CMS should consider requiring that plans develop electronic pathways that 
allow for additional flexibility or exceptions for clearly urgent clinical circumstances. 
 
Additionally, we note that denied prior authorization requests often lead to increased 
complexity for providers who must then appeal the negative decision. Appeals are often 
clinically complex requiring specific appeal arguments and documentation with considerable 
effort required of the provider and their administrative staff. We encourage the agency to 
consider these pitfalls of the prior authorization process if the new regulations are finalized. 
 
Ultimately, many items and services should be able to receive prior authorizations in real-time 
due to the electronic nature of the ePA process. Real-time decisions, when the physician is at

the bedside or exam table also support care coordination and collaborative decision-making 
between the patient and the provider. Real-time decisions also allow patients to receive 
services and treatments immediately, benefitting all patients, especially those that travel long 
distances to receive healthcare, particularly in rural areas. Patients would also be able to 
receive care without needing to take off additional time from work. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comments on these issues critical to the care our members 
provide to their patients. If you need additional information or have questions, please contact 
Joshua J. Webster, Director of Public Policy & Advocacy for the AUA at JWebster@auanet.org. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Mark T. Edney, MD, MBA 
Chair, AUA Public Policy Council 
American Urological Association
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** American Urological Association (AUA); signed by Mark T. Edney, MD, MBA, Chair, AUA Public Policy Council.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association; Healthcare Provider representative.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** AUA states it has more than 22,000 members in more than 100 countries, including more than 18,000 U.S.-based members, representing urologic disease treatment expertise.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

AUA supports modernizing electronic prior authorization for drugs, especially inclusion of physician-administered drugs, because urologists report high PA burden and patient delays for medications and therapies. It asks CMS to standardize PA drug classes, preserve rapid access for time-sensitive therapies, consider urgent exceptions or real-time decisions, and account for appeals burden.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS/Reporting Metrics generally; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** None specifically cited.
- **Standards referenced:** Electronic prior authorization (ePA); interoperability; no FHIR IG, NCPDP, HL7, or CFR citation is specifically named.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic prior authorization expansion to prescription and physician-administered drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** AUA states that standardized ePA and interoperability can reduce administrative burden and improve timely access to drugs and therapies for urologic conditions. It strongly supports including physician-administered drugs such as chemotherapy and infused or injected therapies.
- **Specific request:** Finalize ePA expansion for drugs, including physician-administered drugs furnished in physician offices.

**Topic 2: Standardized drug classes requiring PA**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** AUA understands CMS does not intend to create an exhaustive list of drugs requiring PA but says standardizing drug classes would give providers up-front information and reduce workflow burden.
- **Specific request:** CMS should consider standardizing drug classes that require prior authorization.

**Topic 3: Decision timeframes and urgent clinical exceptions**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support/Modify
- **Rationale:** AUA supports 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited decision timeframes but says some clinical situations require even faster action, including obstructing kidney stones, cancer therapies, and other time-sensitive treatments.
- **Specific request:** Require plans to develop electronic pathways with flexibility or exceptions for clearly urgent clinical circumstances and support real-time decisions when feasible.

**Topic 4: Appeals burden after denials**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Denied PA requests often require clinically complex appeals and extensive documentation by physicians and staff.
- **Specific request:** CMS should consider appeals complexity and downstream provider burden if finalizing new PA regulations.

**Topic 5: Shared decision-making and provider-patient relationship**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Oppose/Concerned
- **Rationale:** AUA states that prior authorization in any form disrupts and interferes with shared decision-making, which it views as fundamental to patient-provider relationships and outcomes.
- **Specific request:** Reduce PA burden and avoid policies that interfere with patient-provider clinical decision-making.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** Supports expanding ePA to medical benefit drugs and specifically physician-administered drugs, including chemotherapy and infused or injected therapies.
- **S15:** Addresses medical benefit drug inclusion by emphasizing physician-administered drugs in office settings and the need for standardized handling of time-sensitive therapies.
- **S20/S43:** Supports 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited timelines but asks CMS to consider faster or real-time pathways for urgent clinical situations.
- **S21:** Implied support for implementation of ePA expansion, but with attention to practical workflow and urgent exception pathways rather than a specific compliance-date request.
- **S29-S30/S34-S35:** The heading references reporting metrics, but the substantive comment focuses mainly on decision timeframes and real-time decisions rather than detailed API usage metrics.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize ePA expansion to prescription drugs and physician-administered medical benefit drugs.
2. Standardize clinical indications for time-sensitive therapies and rapid PA decisions across plans.
3. Consider standardizing drug classes that require prior authorization.
4. Maintain 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited maximum decision timeframes.
5. Require electronic pathways for urgent clinical exceptions and additional flexibility.
6. Encourage real-time PA decisions where the electronic process can support them.
7. Account for appeals burden and documentation complexity caused by denials.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Prior authorization burdens physicians and staff, delays medically necessary urologic medications and therapies, interferes with shared decision-making, and creates complex appeal burdens.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Delayed cancer treatment, delayed access to therapies for overactive bladder, erectile dysfunction, low testosterone, cancer, and benign prostatic hyperplasia; harm from delayed imaging or treatment for obstructing kidney stones; extra travel/time burdens for rural patients and working patients.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Lack of up-front clarity on drugs requiring PA, plan variation, appeal complexity, and absence of pathways for urgent or real-time decisions.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Recent AUA survey data found 93 percent of respondents indicated that medications they prescribe require prior authorization. AUA cites more than 22,000 members, including more than 18,000 in the United States.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Krambeck et al., Campbell-Walsh Urology, cited regarding obstructing kidney stones and morbidity.
- **Examples provided:** PA for medications treating overactive bladder, erectile dysfunction, low testosterone, cancer, and benign prostatic hyperplasia; physician-administered chemotherapy and infused/injected therapies; CT or MRI scans for acute obstructing kidney stones.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Urologists, physician office staff, patients with urologic conditions, rural patients, payers, CMS, and plans implementing ePA workflows.
- **Economic implications:** The comment does not quantify costs, but indicates administrative burden from PA and appeals consumes physician and staff resources and may require additional patient visits or time away from work.
- **Technical feasibility:** AUA views ePA as capable of supporting standardization and possibly real-time decisions, but asks CMS to require pathways for urgent cases.
- **Patient care impact:** Delays can affect cancer treatment, stone disease, medication access, quality of life, continuity of care, and shared decision-making.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive of ePA expansion but concerned about PA burden
- **Tone:** Professional, clinical, and advocacy-oriented
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "prior authorization requirements impose significant administrative burdens" - Context: Establishes AUA's broad concern with PA.
2. "93 percent of respondents indicated that medications they prescribe require prior authorization" - Context: Quantifies burden among AUA members.
3. "strongly supports the inclusion of physician-administered drugs" - Context: Supports PA-DRUG-MEDICAL expansion.
4. "many items and services should be able to receive prior authorizations in real-time" - Context: Supports more rapid electronic PA pathways.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - The comment focuses on administrative burden for physicians and staff, including appeals.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - AUA discusses ePA, interoperability, electronic urgent pathways, and real-time decision potential.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - The comment centers on avoiding delays in medically necessary drugs, therapies, imaging, and procedures.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - AUA asks CMS to standardize plan approaches for drug classes, indications, and rapid decisions.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Standardized drug classes and clinical indications would make PA requirements more predictable.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - AUA specifically highlights physician-administered medical benefit drugs alongside prescription drugs.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment addresses prescribing workflows, bedside/exam-table decisions, appeals, and patient travel/work constraints.
